steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Smart materials: change properties in response to stimuli — thermochromic (temperature), photochromic (light), shape-memory alloys (heat returns original shape).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Nanomaterials: engineered at 1–100 nm scale — graphene (200x stronger than steel, conductive, flexible), carbon nanotubes, nano-coatings.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Composites: two or more materials combined for superior properties — carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) for lightweight strength, fibreglass for boat hulls.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Hydrogel: water-absorbing polymer — used in contact lenses, wound dressings, agriculture (slow-release water), disposable nappies.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe how a shape-memory alloy works and give one practical application. | Explain why graphene is considered a 'wonder material' and discuss the barriers to its widespread use. | Compare a composite material with a single material for use in a bicycle frame.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: A shape-memory alloy (e.g. Nitinol) can be deformed at room temperature and returns to its original shape when heated above a transition temperature. Application: stents in medical surgery that expand | Graphene is incredibly strong (200x steel), lightweight, conductive (electricity and heat), flexible and transparent — potential uses in electronics, energy storage, filtration. Barriers: mass product | CFRP composite frame: extremely light, high strength-to-weight ratio, vibration damping, corrosion resistant — but expensive, difficult to repair, not recyclable. Aluminium frame: affordable, recyclab

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Define the material first, then describe its properties, then give applications — this three-step approach scores full marks Know the difference between 'smart' (responsive) and 'modern' (recently developed) materials Always link material properties to the product function
